lesson.title: What's In The Beaker: The Logic of Qualitative Analysis
lesson.summary: Qualitative analysis uses predicted reactions, especially precipitation, as diagnostic tests to determine which ions are present in an unknown sample.
lesson.body:
Qualitative analysis is the systematic process of figuring out which ions or compounds are present in an unknown sample, as opposed to quantitative analysis, which asks how much of something is present. It leans directly on reaction prediction: every test in a qualitative scheme is really just a predicted reaction, run on purpose, where the appearance, or absence, of a precipitate, a gas, a color change, or a smell tells you something about what ion must have been in the original sample.

The core strategy is selective precipitation. Rather than testing for every possible ion at once, an analyst adds reagents in a deliberate order, each one designed to remove one group of ions from solution as an insoluble solid while leaving the rest dissolved. Because the solubility rules predict exactly which combinations of ions form precipitates, they double as a roadmap for which reagent will isolate which ion. A confirmatory test then follows: a second, more specific reaction, or a physical test like a flame test, that confirms the identity of what precipitated, since more than one ion can sometimes give a similarly colored solid.

Qualitative analysis is also quantitative in disguise more often than the name suggests, because a precipitate's mass is itself evidence. Suppose an unknown white solid is suspected to be a simple chloride salt. A chemist dissolves 0.400 g of the sample in water and adds excess silver nitrate solution, which precipitates all the chloride as white silver chloride: Ag+(aq) + Cl-(aq) -> AgCl(s). After filtering, drying, and weighing, the precipitate has a mass of 0.981 g. The moles of AgCl formed are 0.981 g / 143.32 g/mol = 6.845 x 10^-3 mol, and since each mole of AgCl contains exactly one mole of chloride, the sample contained 6.845 x 10^-3 mol x 35.45 g/mol = 0.2427 g of chlorine by mass.

Dividing that mass of chlorine by the original sample mass gives the percent chlorine by mass in the unknown: 0.2427 g / 0.400 g x 100 = 60.7 percent. That number is not just a percentage, it is a fingerprint. Sodium chloride is 60.66 percent chlorine by mass, an almost exact match, while calcium chloride, at 63.9 percent, and potassium chloride, at 47.6 percent, are clearly different. The mass data alone strongly suggests sodium chloride, though a careful analyst would not stop there: a positive result from one test narrows the possibilities, but confirming the identity of the cation, in this case sodium, calls for an independent physical test.

That is the real lesson of qualitative analysis: no single test is fully conclusive on its own. A precipitate tells you what anion is likely present and roughly how much of it there is, but identifying the full compound usually requires combining a precipitation test with at least one other independent line of evidence.
